programme: RBPJ (CSL/CBF1), the obligate transcriptional effector of canonical Notch signaling — its own target set includes HES1, HEY1, HEY2, NOTCH1, NOTCH3, DLK1 and LFNG, the canonical Notch output genes — acting together with KAT5 (Tip60), a chromatin-acetylation coactivator recruited to Notch/RBPJ target loci, and ZFHX3, which converges independently on the same pericyte-contractility node that RBPJ regulates in cerebral vessels.
role_in_a: In bladder cancer the retrieved evidence places RBPJ in tumor-cell-intrinsic growth control (RITA1 recruits TRIM25 to drive proteasomal turnover in an RBPJ-linked axis, PMID 35701858) and KAT5 among druggable urological-cancer risk genes identified by Mendelian randomization (PMID 42098041) — a growth/proliferation role for this node, not a vascular one.
role_in_b: In stroke the same node operates on the cerebral microvasculature: Rbpj loss disrupts vascular remodeling via Apelin/Cdc42 (PMID 37051908) and impairs pericyte-endothelial communication (PMID 36147294), with region-specific CNS macrophage states also Rbpj-dependent (PMID 39890825); ZFHX3 silencing independently protects against ischemic stroke by suppressing pericyte contraction and calcium influx (PMID 40602592), converging on the same pericyte node; KAT5 knockdown reduces microglial inflammatory injury after acute cerebral ischemia (PMID 40675266).
shared_axis: No source here states bladder cancer and stroke share this pathway; the connection is that RBPJ/Notch, reinforced by its Tip60/KAT5 coactivator, is repeatedly co-opted as a growth-and-remodeling checkpoint in whatever tissue it sits in — tumor-intrinsic proliferation control in bladder urothelium, pericyte-endothelial vascular integrity in cerebral vessels — so the same regulatory node recurs for two different downstream purposes rather than one shared disease mechanism.
reasoning: RBPJ and KAT5 are each placed directly in both diseases by retrieved papers, and ZFHX3 is placed in stroke, so the module is not merely inferred — but the bladder-cancer role documented (RITA1/TRIM25 proteasomal regulation, druggable-genome risk) and the stroke role documented (pericyte-endothelial/vascular remodeling) are mechanistically distinct sub-programmes of the same node, so the cross-disease bridge itself rests on reasoning about Notch's general reuse, not on a retrieved source connecting the two diseases directly.
support: PMID 35701858 — RBPJ-linked RITA1/TRIM25 axis drives bladder cancer cell growth; PMID 39890825 — Rbpj deficiency alters CNS macrophage states relevant to cerebrovascular injury; PMID 37051908 — Rbpj deficiency disrupts vascular remodeling via Apelin/Cdc42; PMID 36147294 — Rbpj loss impairs endothelial cell-pericyte communication; PMID 40602592 — ZFHX3 silencing alleviates ischemic stroke via pericyte contraction/calcium influx; PMID 42098041 — KAT5 among druggable Mendelian-randomization targets in urological cancer; PMID 40675266 — KAT5 knockdown reduces microglial inflammatory injury in acute cerebral ischemia.
how_to_falsify: Delete or dominant-negative RBPJ specifically in bladder tumor epithelium versus cerebral pericytes/mural cells in matched models: if bladder tumor growth is unchanged by RBPJ loss (contradicting the RITA1/TRIM25-dependent mechanism) or pericyte-endothelial coupling and infarct volume are unaffected by Rbpj deletion, the shared-node account fails. Separately, knock down KAT5 in both contexts and measure RBPJ target genes (HES1, HEY1, HEY2) — if KAT5 loss does not change Notch output in either tissue, the proposed coactivator link is wrong.
caveats: Tissue pairing is bladder epithelium versus peripheral blood, so the cerebrovascular pericyte/endothelial literature cited for stroke comes from mouse brain-vessel models, not necessarily the actual blood transcriptomic signal driving the network's Stroke arm. Concordance is drawn from only 2 independent cohort pairs across 75 patient-group comparisons. KLF5 was explicitly discordant despite strong individual bladder-cancer angiogenesis evidence (VEGFA regulation) and was excluded rather than folded into the story. CXXC1 had the highest concordance (74/75) but no disease-specific literature support in either disease and is left unexplained rather than forced in. Single-view factors (notably EPAS1/HIF2A, a plausible hypoxia/vascular candidate) and tissue-generic immune TFs (SPI1, IRF8, BCL6, CIITA, PRDM1, IKZF1, LITAF, KLF1) were removed before ranking, so an immune- or hypoxia-driven narrative was deliberately unavailable and was not substituted here.
